title: Age and seniority
summary: Who is older often decides how two people speak to each other.
body: In Korea, age and seniority shape everyday language. People use polite speech with anyone older or senior to them, and often with strangers of any age.

That is why a new acquaintance may ask your age or year of birth early on. It is not nosy: it helps them choose the right words and title for you. Korean age used to be counted differently, but since 2023 official documents use your international age.
do: Answer the age question simply, for example with your year of birth.
Use polite 해요 style with anyone older, and with anyone you have just met.
Follow the lead of the oldest or most senior person in a group.
avoid: Starting casual speech with someone older: let them offer first.
Taking the age question as rude.
varies: Younger people, international students and people in English-speaking settings are often more relaxed about this.

title: Titles instead of names
summary: Koreans often call people by a title or role, not by their name alone.
body: Calling an older person by their bare name sounds rude in Korean. Instead people use a role or title, often with the honorific 님: 교수님 (professor), 선생님 (teacher, also used for doctors and other professionals), 사장님 (owner or boss).

Between people of similar age, a name with 씨 is polite. Friends use family-style titles for someone a little older: a man calls an older man 형 and an older woman 누나; a woman calls an older man 오빠 and an older woman 언니.
do: Call professors 교수님, in class and in emails.
Use a full name or given name + 씨 with people your age you do not know well.
Ask a new friend what they would like you to call them.
avoid: Using 씨 with your professor or someone much older.
Using a family name + 씨 on its own (for example 김씨): it can sound rude.

words.meaning: teacher; also doctors and other professionals
polite suffix after a name, for equals
older brother; a man to an older man
older sister; a woman to an older woman

title: Korean names
summary: Family name first, usually three syllables, and a woman keeps her family name when she marries.
body: A Korean name starts with the family name: in 김민수, 김 is the family name and 민수 the given name. Most names have three syllables, a one-syllable family name and a two-syllable given name, though shorter and longer names exist. A few family names such as 김, 이 and 박 are very common, so the given name is what tells people apart.

Women keep their own family name after marriage, and children usually take their father's. Between close friends, a younger friend is called by the given name plus 아 after a consonant or 야 after a vowel: 민준아, 수미야.
do: Use the given name or the full name with 씨 for people your age you do not know well: 민수 씨, 김민수 씨.
Repeat a new name back to check it: 민수 씨 맞아요?
Keep 아 / 야 for close friends who are your age or younger.
avoid: Using 아 / 야 with someone older, even a good friend.
Assuming a married couple shares a family name.

words.meaning: May I ask your name? (to someone older)
calling a close friend: given name + 아 / 야

varies: Some people use an English name or a nickname on campus or at work. Use the name they introduce themselves with.

title: Bowing and two hands
summary: A small bow and using both hands show respect.
body: A slight bow with your greeting is normal: a nod of the head with friends, a deeper bow from the waist for professors and older people. A handshake may come with a small bow too.
When you give or receive something from someone older (a card, a document, a drink), use both hands, or your right hand with your left hand touching your right forearm.
do: Bow slightly when you say 안녕하세요 to staff and professors.
Give and take things from older people with two hands.
avoid: Handing something to a professor with one hand while looking away.
Waving casually at someone much older instead of bowing.

title: Speech levels in real life
summary: Polite speech is the safe default; casual speech is something people agree on.
body: Korean has polite speech (존댓말) and casual speech (반말). With strangers, staff, professors and new classmates, people use the polite 해요 style. The formal 합니다 style is used in announcements, presentations and with very senior people.
Friends of the same age often switch to casual speech after a while, usually when one of them suggests it, for example with 말 놓으세요 ("speak casually to me"). Using 반말 before that can feel rude.
do: Use 해요 style by default. Your learner Korean will be welcomed.
Use 합니다 style for a class presentation or a formal email.
avoid: Copying casual phrases from dramas when talking to strangers.
Switching to 반말 with someone older unless they clearly ask you to.
varies: Some friendly groups switch to casual speech quickly; some people prefer polite speech even with friends.

words.meaning: feel free to speak casually (to me)

title: Starting and finishing a meal
summary: Wait for the eldest to start, and say the two meal phrases.
body: At a meal with older people or seniors, it is polite to wait until the oldest person has started eating. Younger people often set out spoons, chopsticks and water for everyone.
Before eating, people say 잘 먹겠습니다 ("I will eat well"), especially to whoever is paying or cooked. After the meal they say 잘 먹었습니다 ("I ate well").
do: Say 잘 먹겠습니다 before and 잘 먹었습니다 after, especially when someone treats you.
Offer to set out the spoons and chopsticks (they are often in a drawer under the table).
avoid: Starting before your professor or the oldest person at the table.
Leaving the table long before the others in a formal setting.

title: Spoon, chopsticks and shared dishes
summary: Rice and soup with a spoon, side dishes with chopsticks, everything shared.
body: Koreans eat rice and soup with a metal spoon and side dishes with metal chopsticks. The rice bowl usually stays on the table rather than being lifted to the mouth.
Side dishes (반찬) are shared by everyone at the table and are often refilled for free. Stews may be shared from one pot, often with a ladle or separate small bowls.
do: Take side dishes with your chopsticks and eat them from your own bowl or plate.
Ask for more side dishes politely: 반찬 좀 더 주세요.
avoid: Standing chopsticks upright in rice: it looks like an offering at memorial rites.
Digging through a shared dish for the best piece.

title: Pouring drinks
summary: Pour for others, not for yourself, and receive with two hands.
body: When drinks are shared from a bottle, people pour for each other rather than for themselves. When someone older pours for you, hold your glass with both hands.
In traditional settings, younger people turn their head slightly away from seniors when they drink. This applies to soft drinks too: the gesture matters, not the alcohol.
do: Pour for the people next to you when their glass is empty.
Hold your glass with two hands when an older person pours.
avoid: Filling your own glass first while others are empty.
Feeling you must drink alcohol: water or a soft drink is fine for the toast.
varies: Among friends of the same age, most of this relaxes. With professors and seniors, it is followed more.

title: Paying the bill
summary: Pay at the counter, no tipping, and ask to split if you want to.
body: In most restaurants you pay at the counter on the way out, or at a kiosk when you order. Tipping is not expected anywhere.

Often one person pays for the group, especially an older or senior person, and others pay next time. Among students, splitting is also common: one person pays and the others send their share by bank transfer, or each person pays separately at the counter.
do: Take the bill (if there is one) to the counter: 계산해 주세요.
To pay separately, say 따로 계산해 주세요.
Thank the person who treated you: 잘 먹었습니다.
avoid: Leaving a tip on the table.
Arguing for a long time over who pays with a professor; a sincere thank you is enough.

title: Professors and emails
summary: Relations with professors are polite and a little formal.
body: Korean students treat professors with clear respect: they greet them on campus, use 교수님, and write emails in a formal tone. Many UNIST courses are taught in English, so you may write in English, but the same politeness helps.
A good email opens with a greeting, says who you are (name, student number, course) and then asks the question briefly. Thank the professor at the end.
do: Greet your professor if you meet on campus, with a small bow.
Put the course name in the email subject.
Use office hours or email for questions rather than catching them in the corridor.
avoid: One-line emails with no greeting or name.
Messaging a professor late at night unless they said it is fine.
varies: Professors who studied or worked abroad are often more informal. Follow your own professor's style.

words.meaning: student number; also your entry year

title: Group projects
summary: Team projects are common, and they run on group chats.
body: Many courses include team projects (팀 프로젝트, often shortened to 팀플). A team usually makes a group chat on KakaoTalk, picks a leader and divides the work.
Being reachable matters a lot. A quick reply, even "I will check tonight", keeps trust in the team.
do: Say early what you can do well (code, slides, research) and take a clear part.
Reply to the group chat within a day.
Tell the team early if you cannot finish your part on time.
avoid: Disappearing from the chat until the deadline.
Changing someone else's part without asking.

title: Clubs and festivals
summary: Clubs are the easiest way to make Korean friends.
body: Student clubs (동아리) cover sport, music, dance, hobbies, volunteering and study. Most recruit at the start of a semester, often with stalls or posters on campus in the first weeks of March.
Universities usually hold a student festival (축제) in spring, with food stalls run by clubs and concerts. Some clubs also go on a trip together, called MT (엠티).
do: Look for club recruitment in the first two weeks of the semester.
Ask whether a club welcomes exchange students; many do.
Go to the spring festival with classmates.
avoid: Waiting until mid-semester: many clubs stop taking members after recruitment.
varies: Festival dates and club life differ from university to university. Check UNIST's student notices.

title: Seniors and juniors
summary: 선배 and 후배 is a relationship of help and respect.
body: At university, a 선배 is a student who entered before you and a 후배 one who entered after you. Students who entered the same year are 동기.

A 선배 often helps a 후배 with advice about classes and life, and may pay for a meal. A 후배 shows respect with polite speech and thanks. As an exchange student you sit a little outside this system, but knowing it explains a lot.
do: Use polite speech with 선배 unless they ask you to speak casually.
Thank a 선배 who treats you, and offer coffee or a snack another time.
avoid: Assuming a 선배 will always pay: offer, and follow their lead.
varies: How strong this hierarchy is depends a lot on the department and the club.

words.meaning: classmate from the same entry year

title: Dorm rules
summary: Every dorm has written rules. Read them in the first week.
body: University dorms in Korea usually have rules about visitors, cooking, smoking, alcohol and cleaning. Some dorms have an entry curfew or a check-in system. Breaking rules can lead to penalty points.
Shoes come off at the door in Korean homes, and often in dorm rooms too. A shared room needs a short talk with your roommate about lights, alarms and guests.
do: Read the dorm rules (and ask for the English version) when you move in.
Agree with your roommate on quiet times, lights out and visitors early on.
Take your shoes off where others do.
avoid: Bringing guests into the dorm before checking the visitor rules.
Cooking in the room if the rules say no.
varies: Rules differ between universities and between dorm buildings. UNIST's own dorm rules are the ones that count.

title: Noise and quiet hours
summary: Noise between rooms and floors is a common cause of conflict.
body: In Korean apartments and dorms, noise between floors (층간소음) is a well-known source of tension: footsteps, music, late phone calls, chairs dragged across the floor.
Many dorms set quiet hours at night. Even without a rule, keep your voice down late in the evening, especially in corridors and shared rooms.
do: Use headphones for music and videos.
Take late calls outside the room or speak quietly.
Apologise simply if someone mentions noise: 죄송합니다, 조심할게요.
avoid: Long video calls on speaker at night in a shared room.
Walking heavily or dragging furniture late at night.

title: Laundry
summary: Shared machines, Korean buttons and a few simple manners.
body: Dorms usually have a shared laundry room (세탁실). Machines may take coins, a card or an app, and the buttons are often only in Korean.
The main words are short: 세탁 (wash), 헹굼 (rinse), 탈수 (spin), 건조 (dry) and 시작 (start). Take your clothes out soon after the cycle ends so others can use the machine.
do: Take a photo of the machine's buttons and learn the five words above.
Set a timer on your phone and collect your laundry on time.
avoid: Leaving wet laundry in a machine for hours.
Taking someone else's clothes out unless the room has a clear habit for it.

title: Waste sorting and recycling
summary: General waste in official bags, food waste and recyclables separately.
body: Korea sorts household waste carefully. General waste goes in official volume-based bags (종량제 봉투), sold at convenience stores and supermarkets; the price of the bag is the disposal fee, and bags are tied to your city or district.

Food waste (음식물 쓰레기) goes in a separate bin or bag. Recyclables (재활용) are split into types such as plastic, cans, glass, paper and styrofoam. Rinse containers, empty bottles and take labels off plastic bottles. Batteries go in their own collection box.
do: Ask the dorm office where each kind of waste goes, on your first day.
Rinse food containers before putting them in recycling.
Buy the bag type your dorm or district uses.
avoid: Putting general waste in a normal shopping bag: it may not be collected.
Mixing food waste into general waste.
varies: Basic categories are national, but bag colours, food waste systems and collection days differ by city, district and building.

title: What counts as food waste
summary: Food waste is only what an animal could eat, roughly.
body: A rough rule many guides give: food waste is something an animal could eat. Hard things such as bones, shells of shellfish, hard fruit stones, tea bags and coffee grounds usually go in general waste instead.
Drain liquid from food waste first. Some buildings use bins that weigh food waste with a card, others use special bags.
do: Drain soup and liquid before throwing food away.
Ask which system your dorm uses: bin, bag or card.
avoid: Putting chicken bones or egg shells in the food waste bin without checking local rules.
varies: Sources and districts differ on some items (for example egg shells). When in doubt, ask the dorm office.

title: Transit cards
summary: One card for buses and subways almost everywhere in Korea.
body: Most people pay for buses and subways with a transit card such as T-money or Cashbee. You can buy one at a convenience store and top it up (충전) there, usually with cash. Many Korean bank cards also work as transit cards.

Tap the card when you get on, and again when you get off the bus. Tapping off lets the system give you a discounted or free transfer to the next bus or subway within a time limit (often 30 minutes; the exact rules depend on the region).
do: Buy a transit card in your first days and keep some balance on it.
Tap off when you leave the bus, even if the fare does not change.
Look at the K-Pass transit refund scheme once you have a Korean bank card.
avoid: Paying for each bus in cash: some buses no longer accept it, and you lose transfer discounts.
varies: Transfer time limits and discounts vary by region.

title: Taking the bus
summary: Get on at the front, press the bell, get off at the back.
body: City buses are the main transport in Ulsan. Get on at the front door and tap your card; get off at the back door. Press the bell (하차벨) before your stop.
Buses can start and brake quickly, so hold on. Bus stops show route numbers, and screens and announcements give the next stop, often in Korean and English.
do: Check the route on Naver Map or KakaoMap before you leave.
Move towards the back door before your stop.
Keep phone calls short and quiet.
avoid: Sitting in priority seats (노약자석) when someone who needs them might board.
Standing up while the bus is still moving fast if you can wait until it slows.

title: Subways in big cities
summary: Ulsan has no subway, but Busan and Seoul do. Learn exit numbers.
body: Ulsan relies on buses and trains; there is no subway. When you visit Busan or Seoul, the subway is the easiest way around. Lines have numbers and colours, and signs are in Korean and English.
Stations have many numbered exits, and directions are often given as "exit 3" (3번 출구). Let people get off before you get on, and keep pregnant-women and priority seats free.
do: Note the exit number of where you are going.
Stand to the side of the doors and let people off first.
avoid: Eating on the subway, or talking loudly on the phone.
Sitting in seats marked for pregnant women (임산부 배려석) if you are not.

title: Trains and buses between cities
summary: KTX trains and intercity buses connect every city. Book ahead on busy days.
body: High-speed KTX trains (run by Korail) and SRT trains connect the big cities; from Seoul to Ulsan takes a little over 2 hours. Tickets can be booked on the Korail website or app.
Express buses (고속버스) and intercity buses (시외버스) are cheaper and go to many more towns. Around Seollal, Chuseok and long weekends, trains and buses fill up early.
do: Book trains for weekends and holidays several days ahead.
Check whether a bus leaves from the express terminal or the intercity terminal; they can be different places.
avoid: Planning holiday travel on the day itself.

title: Taxis
summary: Taxis are common and fairly cheap. Have the address ready in Korean.
body: You can stop a taxi on the street or call one with an app. Drivers may not speak English, so show the address in Korean or a map pin. Most taxis take cards; fares are by meter, and a late-night surcharge applies.
Fasten your seat belt. When you arrive, you can say where to stop and pay by tapping your card.
do: Save the UNIST and dorm address in Korean on your phone.
Greet the driver (안녕하세요) and say the place: 유니스트로 가 주세요.
avoid: Expecting the driver to know English names of places.
Tipping: it is not expected.

title: Cards and cash
summary: Cards work almost everywhere, but keep a little cash.
body: Korea is close to cashless: shops, cafes, taxis and buses take cards, often with self-service kiosks. Foreign cards usually work in shops, but not always in Korean apps and websites (see the Korea apps guide).
Some market stalls, small restaurants and top-up machines still prefer cash. When you pay by credit card, the cashier may ask 일시불이요? (one payment, no instalments): just say 네.
do: Carry a small amount of cash in won.
Say 네 if asked 일시불이요?
avoid: Relying on one foreign card only: bring a backup.

title: Convenience stores
summary: Open late, everywhere, and much more than a shop.
body: Convenience stores (편의점) are on almost every street, many open 24 hours. Besides snacks and drinks, they sell simple meals, official waste bags and a small range of basic medicines, and you can top up a transit card.
Look for 1+1 (buy one, get one free) and 2+1 deals. Many stores have hot water and a microwave for instant noodles and lunch boxes, and a small table to eat at.
do: Use the 1+1 and 2+1 deals.
Bring your own bag, or answer the bag question: 봉투 필요하세요?
avoid: Leaving rubbish on the eating table: clear it into the bins provided.

words.meaning: shall I heat it up for you? (you will hear this)

title: Markets and everyday shopping
summary: Supermarkets, traditional markets and low-price stores for dorm life.
body: Supermarkets and big stores have fixed prices. Traditional markets (시장) sell fresh food, snacks and cheap meals; cash is handy there, and prices are often written on cards or simply asked.
For dorm items such as hangers, cups and storage boxes, low-price chain stores like Daiso are popular and easy to find.
do: Ask the price first at a market stall: 이거 얼마예요?
Try a market snack: it is a good chance to practise Korean numbers.
avoid: Touching or squeezing fresh food without asking.

title: Delivery culture
summary: Almost anything can be delivered, fast.
body: Food delivery is a big part of Korean life: meals arrive quickly, to homes, dorms and even parks. Groceries and online orders also arrive fast, often the next day.
Delivery apps usually need a Korean phone number and a payment method that works in Korea (see the Korea apps guide). Dorms often have a set pickup spot because drivers cannot enter.
do: Learn your dorm's delivery pickup rules.
Write your address exactly as it appears in Korean.
Add a short request: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 (leave it at the door).
avoid: Leaving empty delivery containers in the corridor: clean and sort them.

title: Making friends
summary: Shared activities and KakaoTalk are how friendships start.
body: Friendships often grow from shared activities: classes, team projects, clubs, sport and language exchange. Swapping KakaoTalk IDs is the normal next step.
A phrase like 다음에 밥 한번 먹어요 ("let's eat together sometime") is warm but not a fixed plan. If you would like to meet, suggest a day and a place.
do: Join a club or language exchange in your first weeks.
Suggest a concrete plan: 금요일에 같이 점심 먹을래요?
Use a little Korean, even if the talk continues in English.
avoid: Taking 다음에 밥 한번 먹어요 as a firm promise.
Expecting deep friendship in the first week; it often takes repeated meetings.
varies: People differ: some Korean students are keen to meet international students, others are shy about their English.

title: Group outings
summary: Evenings often move from place to place in rounds.
body: Group dinners for a club, a class or a department are common, especially at the start and end of a semester. An evening may move from dinner (1차, "first round") to a cafe or bar (2차) and further.
You can join the first round and leave politely after it. Say goodbye to the organiser and older people before you go.
do: Join at least the first round of a club or class dinner.
Leave politely: 먼저 가 보겠습니다 (I will head off first).
avoid: Slipping away without saying goodbye to the organiser.

title: Drinking culture and saying no
summary: Alcohol is common at social events, and declining politely is fine.
body: Soju and beer are common at club and department events. Older students may pour for you; you hold your glass with two hands. Your glass may be refilled when it is empty.
You never have to drink. A simple, calm reason works: 저는 술을 안 마셔요 (I do not drink) or 저는 술을 못 마셔요 (I cannot drink). Keeping a soft drink in your glass for the toast is normal.
do: Decide before the event what you will drink.
Say no once, calmly and politely; repeat the same sentence if needed.
Join the toast with a soft drink.
avoid: Drinking more than you want to fit in.
Leaving your drink unattended in a busy bar.
varies: Pressure to drink has decreased a lot, especially among students, but it varies by group.

title: Cafes and study cafes
summary: Cafes are meeting places and study rooms.
body: Korea has cafes everywhere, and many students study in them for hours. It is normal to buy a drink and stay a while.

Study cafes (스터디카페) are quiet rooms where you pay by time at a kiosk; they are popular before exams. Many people leave a bag or laptop on a table to keep a seat; it is common, but keep your phone and passport with you.
do: Buy something if you plan to study in a cafe.
Say whether you are eating in or taking away: 먹고 갈게요 / 포장이요.
avoid: Holding a big table for a long time in a busy cafe with one cheap drink.

title: Seollal (Lunar New Year)
summary: A three-day family holiday, just before you arrive.
body: Seollal (설날) is the Lunar New Year, one of the two biggest holidays. Families gather, younger people bow to their elders (세배) and receive money, and people eat rice cake soup (떡국).

In 2027 the Seollal holiday is 6 to 8 February, with 9 February as a substitute holiday. It is before your arrival on 25 February, but you will hear people talk about it, and the greeting is useful all year round.
do: Learn the greeting 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
Expect busy roads and trains around the holiday in future years.
avoid: Planning a trip on the holiday itself without a booking.

words.meaning: Happy New Year (lit. receive much luck)

title: Chuseok (harvest holiday)
summary: The autumn family holiday, often compared to Thanksgiving.
body: Chuseok (추석) is the harvest festival on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month. Families travel home, remember their ancestors and eat half-moon rice cakes (송편).
In 2027 Chuseok falls on 14 to 16 September, after your semester ends. It is still good to know: it is the time when cities empty out, transport is full and many shops close.
do: Use the greeting 추석 잘 보내세요 (have a good Chuseok) with Korean friends.
avoid: Expecting all shops and restaurants to be open during the holiday.

title: Public holidays in your semester
summary: Five holidays between March and mid-June 2027.
body: Public holidays during the spring 2027 semester (1 March to 18 June): Independence Movement Day (삼일절), Monday 1 March; Labour Day (노동절), Saturday 1 May; Children's Day (어린이날), Wednesday 5 May; Buddha's Birthday (부처님 오신 날), Thursday 13 May; Memorial Day (현충일), Sunday 6 June.

Labour Day became a public holiday for everyone from 2026. Sources did not agree on whether a substitute day off follows when it falls on a Saturday, so check closer to the date. On Memorial Day a siren sounds at 10 a.m. and many people stand for a minute of silence.
do: Check the UNIST academic calendar for class changes around holidays.
Plan trips to Busan or Gyeongju around the 5 May and 13 May holidays, and book early.
avoid: Assuming every office is open on a weekday holiday.
varies: The government can add a temporary holiday at short notice.

title: Cherry blossom season
summary: Spring arrives early in the south, with blossoms soon after you land.
body: Cherry blossoms (벚꽃) open in late March to early April in the south of Korea, usually earlier than in Seoul. They last only a week or two, and parks, rivers and campuses fill with people taking photos.
Many towns hold blossom festivals. Exact dates move every year with the weather, so watch the forecast in March.
do: Plan a walk or trip for the first weekend of blossoms.
Go early in the morning or on a weekday to avoid crowds.
avoid: Breaking branches or climbing trees for photos.
varies: Blossom dates change each year with the weather.

title: Weather and fine dust
summary: Mild spring, dusty days, then a humid early summer.
body: Ulsan is on the south-east coast, so winters are milder than in Seoul, and March can still be cold and windy. Spring days can bring fine dust (미세먼지) and yellow dust (황사), and many people check air quality and wear masks on bad days.
The rainy season (장마) usually starts around late June, near the end of your semester. Summer is hot and humid.
do: Check the air quality in a weather or map app on spring days.
Bring a warm jacket for March and an umbrella for June.
avoid: Long outdoor runs on days with very bad air quality.
varies: Weather varies a lot from year to year.

title: Common dishes
summary: Ten dishes you will see on almost every menu near campus.
body: Everyday favourites: 김밥 (rice rolls), 비빔밥 (mixed rice with vegetables), 김치찌개 (kimchi stew), 된장찌개 (soybean paste stew), 불고기 (marinated beef), 떡볶이 (spicy rice cakes), 라면 (instant noodles), 삼겹살 (grilled pork belly), 치킨 (fried chicken) and 냉면 (cold noodles).
A meal usually comes with rice and several free side dishes. Around UNIST, Eonyang is known for its own style of grilled bulgogi (언양 불고기).
do: Learn to read these ten names on menus: it is great Hangul practice.
Try 김밥 shops for cheap, quick meals.
avoid: Ordering one portion of a dish that is sold for two or more people (common for meat and some stews): check the menu.

title: How spicy is it?
summary: Many dishes are spicy. You can ask, and sometimes choose.
body: Red pepper paste and powder are in many dishes, so a lot of Korean food is spicy. Red colour is a good hint, but not always.
Some restaurants let you choose the spice level. You can ask 많이 매워요? (is it very spicy?) or request 안 맵게 해 주세요 (not spicy, please) or 덜 맵게 해 주세요 (less spicy).
do: Ask before ordering if you do not like spicy food.
Order a mild dish alongside a spicy one when sharing.
avoid: Assuming a dish is mild because it is white or clear.
varies: Not every restaurant can make a dish less spicy.

title: Asking what is in a dish
summary: Useful if you avoid pork, meat, seafood or have an allergy.
body: Many dishes contain ingredients you cannot see: meat or anchovy stock in soups, fermented seafood (젓갈) in kimchi, pork in dumplings. Vegetarian food is possible but takes some asking.
Ask with 들어가요? (does it go in?): 돼지고기 들어가요? (is there pork in it?). For an allergy, say 저는 땅콩 알레르기가 있어요 (I am allergic to peanuts), changing the food word.
do: Learn the Korean words for anything you cannot eat.
For a serious allergy, carry a short note in Korean.
avoid: Relying on the menu photo alone.

words.meaning: is it in it? (lit. does it go in?)

title: Campus cafeteria meals
summary: Cheap set meals on a tray: rice, soup, a main and side dishes.
body: University cafeteria food (학식) is the cheapest way to eat well. A typical tray (식판) holds rice, soup, kimchi, two or three side dishes and a main dish. The menu changes daily and is often posted online.
You may pay at a kiosk, by card or with a meal ticket. After eating, take your tray to the return area and sort leftovers where there are separate bins.
do: Check the day's menu before you go.
Return your tray and sort leftovers as others do.
avoid: Leaving your tray on the table.
varies: Payment and menus differ by campus and by cafeteria.

title: Ordering at a kiosk
summary: Touchscreen kiosks are everywhere. Six words get you through.
body: Many restaurants, cafes and fast food places take orders at a touchscreen kiosk. Some have an English button, many do not.
The key words: 주문 (order), 매장 (eat in), 포장 (takeaway), 결제 (payment), 카드 (card) and 취소 (cancel). After paying you usually get a number; listen for it or watch the screen.
do: Look for an English or language button first (often a globe icon).
Ask staff if stuck: 이거 어떻게 해요? (how do I do this?).
avoid: Panicking if people queue behind you: take your time or step aside.

title: Indirect answers
summary: A clear "no" is often softened.
body: Many Koreans avoid a direct "no", especially with people they do not know well or with seniors. Phrases like 좀 어려울 것 같아요 ("it seems a bit difficult") or 생각해 볼게요 ("I will think about it") often mean no.
Likewise, 괜찮아요 can mean "it is fine" or "no, thank you", depending on the situation and tone.
do: Listen for softeners and accept a soft no without pushing.
Soften your own refusals: 죄송한데, 좀 어려울 것 같아요.
avoid: Asking the same request again and again after a soft no.
varies: People who are close, or who have lived abroad, are often more direct.

words.meaning: it seems a bit difficult (often a polite no)

title: Nunchi: reading the room
summary: Noticing what others feel and expect, without being told.
body: 눈치 is the skill of sensing a situation: noticing when someone is busy, when a group wants to leave, or when a joke does not fit. Someone with good 눈치 adjusts without being asked.
As a newcomer, you are not expected to know everything. Watching what others do and asking quietly when unsure is a good way to show it.
do: Watch how others behave in a new place, then follow.
Ask quietly if unsure: 이렇게 하면 돼요? (is it okay like this?).
avoid: Worrying too much: people are usually patient with foreigners.

title: Messaging habits
summary: KakaoTalk is where daily life happens.
body: Almost everyone uses KakaoTalk for chats, group projects, clubs and even notices from shops. A small number next to a message shows how many people have not read it yet.
Common text shortcuts: ㅋㅋ (laughing), ㅎㅎ (a softer smile), ㅠㅠ (crying, sad or touched). They are casual: use them with friends, not with professors.
do: Reply within a day in group chats.
Keep messages to professors and staff formal and complete.
avoid: Using ㅋㅋ or emoticons in messages to professors.
Leaving messages read without reply for days in a team chat.

title: Softening requests
summary: A few small words make any request polite.
body: Koreans soften requests with small words: 좀 (a little), 혹시 (by any chance), and openers like 죄송한데요 (sorry, but...). For example: 혹시 사진 좀 찍어 주실 수 있어요? (Could you possibly take a photo for me?).
To get a stranger's or a waiter's attention, say 저기요 (excuse me). 실례합니다 is used when interrupting or passing through.
do: Start requests to strangers with 저기요 or 죄송한데요.
Add 좀 to requests: 물 좀 주세요.
avoid: Calling out 야 (hey): it is rude to strangers.

title: Emergency numbers
summary: 112 police, 119 fire and ambulance, 1330 and 1345 for help in English.
body: 112 is the police; 119 is fire and ambulance. Both work from any phone, free.

For non-emergency help in English and other languages: 1330 is the Korea Travel Helpline (tourism information and interpretation; from a mobile, an area code may be needed, for example 02-1330), and 1345 is the Immigration Contact Center for visa and residence questions.
do: Save 112, 119, 1330 and 1345 in your phone before you fly.
Know your dorm address in Korean so you can give it on the phone.
avoid: Waiting to call 119 because of language: say the address and 영어 (English) and stay on the line.

title: Pharmacies
summary: For small problems, a pharmacist is the first stop.
body: Pharmacies (약국) are easy to find by the large 약 sign. Pharmacists can suggest medicine for colds, headaches, stomach problems and small cuts; describe your symptoms simply or show a translation.
Late at night, convenience stores sell a small range of basic medicines such as fever and pain relief. Prescription medicine needs a doctor's prescription.
do: Bring any regular medicine from home with its name in English.
Use simple sentences: 머리가 아파요 (I have a headache), 열이 나요 (I have a fever).
avoid: Taking medicine you cannot read without asking the pharmacist.

title: If you are sick
summary: Small clinics for everyday illness, the emergency room for emergencies.
body: For a cold, flu or a stomach bug, people go to a local clinic (의원 or 병원), often an internal medicine clinic (내과) or an ear, nose and throat clinic (이비인후과). Small clinics usually see walk-in patients; bring your passport or residence card.
For serious emergencies go to an emergency room (응급실) or call 119. Health insurance rules for international students depend on your visa and length of stay, so ask UNIST before you arrive.
do: Ask UNIST about health insurance and any campus health service before you arrive.
Keep receipts: your travel or student insurance may refund costs.
avoid: Going to a big hospital's emergency room for a mild cold: it is slow and costly.

title: Emergency alerts on your phone
summary: Loud phone alerts warn about weather, disasters and other dangers.
body: Korean phones receive emergency text alerts (재난문자) from the government and local authorities: heavy rain, typhoons, earthquakes, fire, very bad air quality or a missing person. Some come with a loud alarm.
Alerts may be only in Korean. Copy the text into a translator to see whether you need to act. The Korea apps guide lists a government safety app with alerts in English.
do: Translate an alert as soon as it arrives.
Follow official instructions, such as staying indoors in a typhoon.
avoid: Switching off all alerts on your phone.

title: Ulsan, the city
summary: An industrial city on the south-east coast, with mountains, a river and the sea.
body: Ulsan (울산) is a metropolitan city of about 1.1 million people on Korea's south-east coast, between Busan and Gyeongju. It is a centre of Korean industry: car making, shipbuilding and petrochemicals.
The Taehwa River (태화강) runs through the city, with a large riverside garden. Ulsan has no subway: people use city buses, and the Donghae Line train connects Taehwagang Station with Busan.
do: Learn the names of a few districts: 삼산동 (shopping area), 태화강 (the river), 언양 (the town near UNIST).
Use Naver Map or KakaoMap for bus routes.
avoid: Expecting Seoul-style late-night transport everywhere: check the last bus.

title: UNIST and Eonyang
summary: The campus is in Eonyang, west of the city centre, close to the KTX station.
body: UNIST (울산과학기술원, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology) is at 50 UNIST-gil, Eonyang-eup, Ulju-gun, Ulsan. It is outside the busy city centre, near the town of Eonyang (언양) and the KTX Ulsan Station.
Many UNIST courses are taught in English. The International Affairs Team looks after exchange students: check its pages for orientation, housing and buddy information before you fly.
do: Save the campus address in Korean: 울산광역시 울주군 언양읍 유니스트길 50.
Read the inbound exchange pages of the International Affairs Team.
avoid: Booking accommodation in the city centre for your first night without checking travel time to campus.

title: From the airport to Ulsan
summary: From Incheon: train via Seoul Station, or a direct bus. From Gimhae: about an hour by bus.
body: From Incheon Airport, the usual route is the airport railroad (AREX) to Seoul Station, then a KTX to Ulsan (울산역, also signed 통도사). The KTX part takes a little over 2 hours. The direct KTX from the airport stopped in 2018, though some old guides still mention it.

Direct intercity buses run from Incheon Airport (both terminals) to Ulsan several times a day, about 5 hours, with no change and room for luggage. Domestic flights also link Gimpo Airport (Seoul) and Ulsan Airport. If you land at Gimhae Airport (Busan), an airport limousine bus reaches Ulsan in about an hour.
do: Book the KTX or bus ahead, and leave at least 2 to 3 hours after landing for immigration and luggage.
Check current times on Korail and the bus booking sites a week before you fly.
Ask UNIST if there is an airport pickup for exchange students.
avoid: Following old guides that mention a direct KTX from Incheon Airport.
Confusing KTX Ulsan Station with Taehwagang Station in the city centre.

title: From KTX Ulsan Station to campus
summary: About 10 to 15 minutes by taxi, or a short bus ride.
body: KTX Ulsan Station is in the Eonyang area, close to UNIST. A taxi takes about 10 to 15 minutes; fares were around ₩8,000 to ₩9,000 at the last check, more late at night.
City buses also link the station and campus. UNIST's directions name route 337; check the current route in Naver Map or KakaoMap before you travel.
do: Take a taxi on arrival day if you have heavy luggage: show 유니스트 and the dorm name.
Learn the bus route for later trips to the station.
avoid: Leaving the station for the city centre first: it is in the other direction.

title: Places to see in Ulsan
summary: A river garden, a coastal park, a sunrise cape and ancient rock carvings.
body: Taehwagang National Garden (태화강 국가정원) follows the river through the city, with a bamboo forest walk. Daewangam Park (대왕암공원) has pine forest paths and a bridge over sea rocks. Ganjeolgot (간절곶) is a cape famous for sunrises.

The Bangudae petroglyphs, rock carvings of whales and hunting thousands of years old, were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 as the Petroglyphs along the Bangucheon Stream. They are in Ulju County, like UNIST. Mountain lovers can hike the Yeongnam Alps (영남알프스) nearby.
do: Visit the river garden and the bamboo forest on a spring weekend.
Check opening times on the Ulsan tourism site before you go.
avoid: Leaving marked paths on coastal rocks, especially in wind.

title: Day trip: Busan
summary: Korea's second city, beaches and markets, about an hour away.
body: Busan (부산) is Korea's second-largest city and its biggest port. Popular spots include Haeundae beach, Gamcheon Culture Village and Jagalchi fish market. It has a subway, which makes getting around easy.
From Ulsan, the Donghae Line commuter train runs from Taehwagang Station to Busan (Bujeon), about 76 minutes end to end. Intercity buses and KTX trains are other options.
do: Go on a weekday or early on a weekend to avoid crowds.
Top up your transit card: it works on Busan's buses and subway.
avoid: Trying to see all of Busan in one day: pick one area.

title: Day trip: Gyeongju
summary: The ancient Silla capital, just north of Ulsan.
body: Gyeongju (경주) was the capital of the Silla kingdom for about a thousand years. Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto, and the Gyeongju Historic Areas, are UNESCO World Heritage sites.

In the centre, the large grass-covered royal tombs of Daereungwon (대릉원) and the old observatory Cheomseongdae (첨성대) are within walking or cycling distance. Bulguksa is further out, so plan a bus or taxi.
do: Rent a bicycle to see the central sites.
Start early: Bulguksa is busy at weekends.
avoid: Climbing on the tombs: they are protected heritage.
